newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil early May trade surplus is no surprise.
newsitem.headline: Brazil early May trade surplus is no surprise.

text.p: Data showing Brazil posted a small trade surplus in the first two weeks of May came as no surprise and confirmed views that this month's trade figures should show a significant improvement, analysts said.
Analysts said seasonal factors best explained the $77 million trade surplus for the first six days of May which was announced earlier on Tuesday by the Ministry of Industry and Commerce.
"Daily imports are somewhat lower than what we had expected and exports are always strong at this time of the year," said Thomas Malaga an economist at Unibanco.
Malaga warned against reading too much into the new data. "I think this was widely expected. I continue to forecast a trade deficit of between $100 million and $200 million in May."
The Industry and Commerce Ministry said exports for the first six days of the month totalled $1.418 billion against imports of $1.341 billion.
The ministry said average daily exports for the month so far stood at $236.3 million while average daily imports were $223.5 million.

Brazil's trade balance has become one of the country's most closely-watched economic indicators after the trade gap for the first four months of this year reached almost $4 billion against $5.54 billion for all of 1996.
Analysts said Brazil traditionally shows strong exports between May and August, when the bulk of the agricultural harvest is shipped.
They said those figures would be strengthened this year by excellent commoditiy prices, particularly for soybeans, coffee and orange juice, three of Brazil's main exports.
Ana Cristina Goncalves da Costa of consultants MCM said today's data could also be a sign that government efforts to correct the trade balance may have begun to kick in.

She said the lower imports could be a result of the Central Bank's decision last March to restrict import financing to 360 days and a recognition by businessmen that 1997 growth would be slower than originally expected.
"There is no doubt that demand is weaker," Goncalves said.
None of the analysts consulted by Reuters said the new data were enough for them to alter their 1997 trade balance forecasts.
Local investment houses are predicting Brazil will post a 1997 trade deficit in a range between $9.0 billion and $13 billion.
